question: Design a secure, performant solution for enforcing field-level security in a scoped ServiceNow application where some fields on an Incident-derived custom table must be editable only by a specific business role, while other fields remain editable by the assigned incident handler. Explain how you would use ACLs, Business Rules, and client-server interactions to implement this, describe pitfalls to avoid, and how you'd test and validate the solution.
answer:
Answer:

Approach (high level)

  • Use table- and field-level ACLs for authoritative server-side enforcement of who can read/update sensitive fields.
  • Use Business Rules (server-side) to enforce additional business logic and data integrity when records change.
  • Use client scripts or UI Policies for UX (hide/disable fields) but never as the only security control.
  • Use glideAjax or async server calls if the client needs permission info that depends on server-side logic.

Detailed design

  1. Create granular field ACLs (update and read) on the scoped custom table for each protected field; ACL conditions should check roles or a function that evaluates complex rules.
    ACL: table: x_myapp_incident.fieldX, operation: update, script: answer(gs.hasRole('u_sensitive_editor'))
  2. Implement Business Rules before/after update (server-side) to validate state transitions or enforce cross-field invariants; set advanced conditions to minimize overhead and make them non-async unless needed.
    BR (before update): if (!gs.hasRole('u_sensitive_editor') && current.fieldX.changes()) gs.addErrorMessage('Not allowed'); current.fieldX = previous.fieldX;
  3. On the client, use UI Policy/Client Script to disable or hide fields based on a permission check obtained via a secure glideAjax script include that runs server-side logic to return permission booleans. Cache results briefly to avoid extra calls.
    Client: var permis = new GlideAjax('PermUtils'); permis.getXMLAnswer('canEditFieldX', callback);
Server SI: canEditFieldX -> return gs.hasRole('u_sensitive_editor');
  4. Scoped app considerations: implement ACLs and Script Includes as application-scoped and mark Script Includes as accessible to the scope that needs them; avoid global-only constructs and follow scoped best practices.

Pitfalls to avoid

  • Relying solely on client-side disabling — that can be bypassed; ACLs are mandatory for security.
  • Creating expensive Business Rules or ACL scripts that run on every record without good conditions (use conditions to limit execution).
  • Using gs.hasRole in many places without a central utility — consolidate logic to a single Script Include for maintainability.
  • Not accounting for background scripts, integrations, or impersonation — ensure ACL logic covers system roles and integration users appropriately.

Testing and validation

  • Unit tests: create automated server-side tests (ATF) to confirm ACLs block/allow updates for users with and without roles.
  • Integration tests: simulate API calls and background jobs to verify ACLs and Business Rules behave for non-interactive users.
  • UI tests: validate client-side disabling matches server-side enforcement (attempt direct REST/GlideRecord writes to confirm ACLs block them).
  • Performance checks: load-test common operations and review ACL/BR execution traces; optimize by narrowing conditions and caching permission calls where safe.

question: Design an asynchronous integration pattern in ServiceNow using Flow Designer and IntegrationHub to call an external REST API that returns large datasets and rate-limits requests. Describe the end-to-end design, failure and retry handling, data ingestion into CMDB (or a scoped table), and how you would monitor and troubleshoot the process.
answer:
Answer (senior-level): Provide an event-driven, chunked-fetch asynchronous flow using IntegrationHub spokes, message queues, and background processing to reliably ingest large, rate-limited REST responses into ServiceNow.

Design overview

  • Trigger: scheduled Flow Designer flow or inbound webhook that starts the sync and creates a Sync Control record to store metadata (cursor, batch size, rate-limit state).
  • Chunked retrieval: Flow invokes an IntegrationHub REST action that requests a single page/batch from the external API using the Sync Control cursor and configured pageSize.
  • Asynchronous processing: For each retrieved batch, the flow enqueues a background Processing Context (create a Flow Execution or use event queue/message queue) to transform and upsert records to the target table (CMDB or scoped table) using glideRecord/upsert-like actions provided by IntegrationHub or a custom action.
  • Rate-limit enforcement: After each API call, read response headers (e.g., X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After). If remaining is low or 429 returned, update Sync Control and schedule a delayed retry (use Flow Designer Delay action or a scheduled job) honoring Retry-After.
  • Continuation: If API returns nextCursor/nextPage, update Sync Control and re-trigger the chunk-fetch flow until completion. Mark Sync Control complete when no cursor remains.

Failure & retry handling

  • Idempotency: Use a unique external ID (composite key) to upsert records to avoid duplicates on retries.
  • Retries: For transient network/5xx errors, implement exponential backoff and limited retry counts in the flow; persist retry count and lastError in Sync Control.
  • Poison handling: After max retries, move batch detail to an error queue/table with context for manual review and alerting.
  • Transactional safety: Perform per-record upserts so a failed record does not abort the entire batch; collect failures for reprocessing.

Data ingestion & mapping

  • Transformation: Use IntegrationHub Transform map or a custom action to map external fields to CMDB schema; apply normalization/lookup (CI type, owner) within the processing action.
  • Bulk vs single upserts: Prefer batched upsert actions if available for performance, otherwise process records in controlled parallelism (e.g., 5 concurrent processors) to avoid hitting rate or DB contention.

Monitoring & troubleshooting

  • Operational records: Sync Control stores state (startedAt, lastRun, lastCursor, status, errors). Batch records store per-batch status, counts, and sample errors.
  • Logging: Capture request/response headers, response payload sizes, and external error codes in log entries (respecting PII/security).
  • Alerts & dashboards: Create dashboards showing success rate, throughput, rate-limit events, error queue length; alert on repeated 429s or growing error queue.
  • Debugging: Enable Flow execution details, use IntegrationHub action logs, and replay failed batches via a reprocess action that reuses saved payloads and cursor state.

Additional considerations

  • Security: Store API credentials in Credential record and use scoped credentials; enforce least privilege and encryption at rest/in transit.
  • Performance & limits: Respect instance transaction limits and background processing quotas—use asynchronous Flow executions and avoid long-running synchronous actions.
  • Extensibility: Encapsulate REST call and upsert logic into reusable Actions/Subflows so other integrations can reuse paging, rate-limit, and retry logic.
Example pseudocode action call:
callRestPage({cursor: sync.cursor, pageSize:50})
processBatch(batch.records)
if(batch.nextCursor) scheduleNext(batch.nextCursor)

question: Explain the difference between GlideRecord and GlideAggregate. When would you use one over the other, and what are the performance implications?
answer:
GlideRecord retrieves individual records and loads all fields into memory. GlideAggregate performs database-level aggregations (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) without loading record data.

Performance Implications:

  • GlideRecord COUNT anti-pattern: gr.query(); while(gr.next()) count++; loads every record into memory - O(n) memory and time.
  • GlideAggregate: ga.addAggregate('COUNT'); ga.query(); executes a single SQL COUNT - O(1) memory.

Code Example:

// ❌ Bad - Loads 100K records into memory
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('state', 1);
gr.query();
var count = gr.getRowCount(); // Still bad!

// ✅ Good - Single DB operation
var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addQuery('state', 1);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.query();
var count = ga.next() ? ga.getAggregate('COUNT') : 0;

When to use GlideAggregate:

  • Counting records
  • Summing numeric fields (e.g., total cost)
  • Finding min/max values
  • GROUP BY operations with addGroupBy()

question: A Business Rule and a Client Script both update the same field. Describe the exact execution order and how to prevent race conditions.
answer:
Execution Order (on form submit):

  1. Client Script (onSubmit) - Runs in browser BEFORE data sent to server
  2. Business Rule (before) - Runs on server BEFORE database write
  3. Database Write - Actual INSERT/UPDATE
  4. Business Rule (after) - Runs AFTER database write
  5. Async Business Rule - Queued, runs independently

Race Condition Scenario:

// Client Script sets priority to 1
g_form.setValue('priority', '1');

// Before BR also sets priority based on impact
current.priority = calculatePriority(current.impact);

The Business Rule always wins because it runs after client script and directly modifies the GlideRecord before DB write.

Prevention Strategies:

  • Single source of truth: Let only BR handle field, use UI Policy for display
  • Use g_scratchpad: Pass client decisions to server
  • Check current.changes(): In BR, respect user changes
// Business Rule - respect user's explicit change
if (!current.priority.changes()) {
  current.priority = calculatePriority(current.impact);
}

question: How does ServiceNow's ACL evaluation work? Explain the order of evaluation and what happens when multiple ACLs match.
answer:
ACL Evaluation Order (most specific to least):

  1. Table.Field - e.g., incident.caller_id (most specific)
  2. Table.* - e.g., incident.* (table wildcard)
  3. *.Field - e.g., *.caller_id (field across tables)
  4. *.* - Global default (least specific)

Multiple ACL Match Rules:

When multiple ACLs match at the same specificity level, they are ANDed together - ALL must pass.

// Two ACLs on incident.* read:
// ACL 1: role = itil
// ACL 2: script checks assignment_group
// User must have itil AND pass the script

Critical Gotcha - The 'admin' Override:

// This ACL will NEVER block admin users!
// Admin bypasses ACL evaluation entirely unless:
gs.hasRole('admin') // Always true for admin

// To restrict even admin, use:
if (gs.hasRole('admin')) return false; // Explicit deny

Debug ACLs:

// Enable ACL debugging for troubleshooting
gs.setProperty('glide.security.debug', 'true');
// Check: System Logs > Security Debug

question: Design a solution to process 50,000 records nightly without causing performance issues or hitting governor limits.
answer:
Key Constraints:

  • Script execution timeout: 5 minutes (configurable)
  • Memory limits per transaction
  • Database connection limits

Solution Architecture:

// 1. Scheduled Job triggers Flow Designer
// 2. Flow uses 'For Each' with batch processing
// 3. Each batch runs as separate transaction

// Scheduled Script:
var workflow = new GlideFlow('process_records_flow');
workflow.startAsync();

Flow Designer Approach:

  1. Query records with setLimit(500) per batch
  2. Use For Each action with parallel execution
  3. Subflow handles individual record processing
  4. Built-in retry and error handling

Alternative - Event-Driven:

// Create events in batches
var gr = new GlideRecord('large_table');
gr.addQuery('processed', false);
gr.setLimit(1000);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  gs.eventQueue('custom.process.record', gr, gr.sys_id, '');
  gr.processed = true;
  gr.setWorkflow(false); // Skip BR
  gr.autoSysFields(false); // Skip sys_updated
  gr.update();
}
// Script Action processes each event async

Performance Tips:

  • setWorkflow(false) - Skip Business Rules
  • autoSysFields(false) - Skip audit fields
  • setLimit() - Always batch
  • Use updateMultiple() for bulk updates

question: Explain ServiceNow's scoped application architecture. How do scope isolation and cross-scope access work?
answer:
Scope Isolation Principles:

  • Each app runs in its own namespace (e.g., x_myco_app)
  • Tables, scripts, and records are scoped by default
  • Global scope can access everything; scoped apps are restricted

Cross-Scope Access Methods:

// 1. Script Include with 'Accessible from' = 'All scopes'
var si = new global.GlobalUtility();

// 2. GlideScriptedProcessor for REST-like access
// 3. Cross-scope API (sn_ws namespace)
// 4. Application Property: glide.script.block.client.globals

Table Access Patterns:

// From scoped app accessing global table:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident'); // Works - incident is global

// From scoped app accessing another scope's table:
var gr = new GlideRecord('x_other_app_table');
// ❌ Fails unless 'Application Access' granted

Granting Cross-Scope Access:

  1. Navigate to target table → Application Access
  2. Enable: Can read / Can create / Can update / Can delete
  3. Or use sys_scope_privilege table

Security Best Practices:

  • Never put sensitive logic in 'Accessible from all scopes'
  • Use GlideScriptedProcessor as API gateway
  • Validate caller scope: gs.getCurrentApplicationScope()

question: What is the 'current' object mutation problem in Business Rules, and how do you solve it?
answer:
The Problem:

In 'before' Business Rules, the current object is mutable and shared across all BRs in the same transaction. One BR's changes affect subsequent BRs.

// BR 1 (Order: 100)
current.short_description = 'Modified by BR1';

// BR 2 (Order: 200) - sees BR1's change!
if (current.short_description.includes('BR1')) {
  // This executes unexpectedly!
}

Why It Happens:

  • current is a reference to the same GlideRecord instance
  • All 'before' BRs share this reference
  • Changes are cumulative until DB write

Solutions:

// 1. Use previous object for original values
if (previous.short_description != current.short_description) {
  // Field actually changed by user
}

// 2. Use changes() method
if (current.short_description.changes()) {
  // User changed this field
}

// 3. Store original in scratchpad (first BR)
if (!current.scratchpad) current.scratchpad = {};
current.scratchpad.original_desc = previous.short_description;

// 4. Check operation type
if (current.operation() == 'insert') {
  // previous is empty on insert
}

Best Practice:

Always use previous object when comparing values, and current.field.changes() to detect user modifications vs BR modifications.

question: How would you implement a custom caching mechanism in ServiceNow to reduce database queries?
answer:
ServiceNow Caching Options:

  1. GlideSystem Cache - gs.getProperty() with caching
  2. Script Include with Static Variables - Session-level
  3. GlideCacheManager - Enterprise cache API
  4. System Properties - Cached by platform

Implementation - Script Include Cache:

var CachedLookup = Class.create();
CachedLookup.cache = {}; // Static - survives instance
CachedLookup.cacheExpiry = {};
CachedLookup.TTL = 300000; // 5 minutes

CachedLookup.prototype = {
  initialize: function() {},
  
  get: function(key) {
    var now = new Date().getTime();
    if (CachedLookup.cache[key] && 
        CachedLookup.cacheExpiry[key] > now) {
      return CachedLookup.cache[key];
    }
    
    // Cache miss - fetch from DB
    var value = this._fetchFromDB(key);
    CachedLookup.cache[key] = value;
    CachedLookup.cacheExpiry[key] = now + CachedLookup.TTL;
    return value;
  },
  
  invalidate: function(key) {
    delete CachedLookup.cache[key];
  },
  
  _fetchFromDB: function(key) {
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_properties');
    gr.get('name', key);
    return gr.value;
  },
  
  type: 'CachedLookup'
};

Caveats:

  • Cache is per-node in clustered environments
  • Use for read-heavy, rarely-changed data
  • Invalidate on relevant Business Rule updates

question: Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous Business Rules. What are the risks of async BRs?
answer:
Synchronous Business Rules:

  • Execute in the same transaction as the triggering event
  • Block until complete
  • Can prevent record save (before) or access updated data (after)

Asynchronous Business Rules:

  • Queue as scheduled jobs
  • Execute in separate transaction
  • Cannot affect the original transaction

Critical Risks of Async BRs:

// RISK 1: Record may be modified/deleted before async runs
// Async BR queued at 10:00:00
// User deletes record at 10:00:01
// Async runs at 10:00:05 - current is stale/gone!

// Solution: Always re-fetch
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (!gr.get(current.sys_id)) {
  return; // Record deleted
}
// RISK 2: No access to 'previous' object
// previous is ALWAYS empty in async BR
if (previous.state != current.state) {
  // ❌ This never works in async!
}
// RISK 3: Transaction isolation
// Async cannot rollback original transaction
// If async fails, original save still committed

When to Use Async:

  • Sending notifications
  • External integrations
  • Heavy processing that shouldn't block UI
  • Audit logging to external systems
